Issued at 152 PM CDT Thu Oct 8 2026

Dry conditions beneath partly cloudy skies continue this afternoon. 
The dry conditions look to persist for the rest of the afternoon and 
into the evening hours before chances for showers and storms return 
to the forecast area. A weak mid level shortwave trough will push 
into the forecast area, strengthening the low level jet (LLJ) and 
low level warm air advection (WAA). The LLJ and WAA will steepen mid 
level lapse rates, resulting in sufficient buoyancy between 700 to 
1,200 J/kg of CAPE. Thus, thunderstorms are expected on the nose of 
the LLJ. Effective shear values will be sufficient at 35 to 40 
knots. The lingering uncertainty is where storms will develop. 
Latest guidance has come in with a further east solution. Should 
this solution pan out, then little to no storms would develop in the 
forecast area. Think the most likely scenario is that the broad WAA 
in place will develop a few storms in the CWA, mainly in northwest 
Iowa this evening and night. A few of these storms could be strong 
to severe with large hail up to the size of ping pong balls. Should 
see storms push east of the forecast area by 5 to 6 am. 

Friday will see warming highs up to the 70s and 80s thanks to the 
previously mentioned WAA. Winds will also be strengthening 
throughout the day as low level pressure gradients tighten with 
southeasterly winds gusting to 20-30 mph. With the tighter pressure 
gradients in place, breezy winds will persist through the evening 
and night, this will keep low temperatures very mild, with lows only 
falling to the 60s overnight. These warm overnight lows will be 
near or may break warm low temperatures records.

The thermal ridge axis will remain parked over the Northern Plains 
on Saturday, resulting in the warmest temperatures over the weekend. 
High temperatures will warm to the 80s across the area with a few 
locations across central and south central South Dakota seeing highs 
potentially reach 90F. These warm high temperatures are near records 
currently. Could see temperatures creep towards record territory if 
highs continue to warm heading into Saturday. The heat will be 
accompanied by stronger southerly winds and lower humidity, yielding 
elevated fire danger across the area. The lowest humidity and 
hottest temperatures continues to look to reside over central and 
south central South Dakota where humidity values look to fall below 
25%. However, winds will be weakening in this area through the 
daylight hours as the low level pressure gradient is shunted a bit 
eastward. Locations along and east of the James River will see the 
strongest winds with gusts up to 30-40 mph. Isolated higher gusts up 
to about 45 mph is possible along the Buffalo Ridge in southwest 
Minnesota. This will result in an offset of the strongest winds and 
lowest humidity. Fuels continue to remain green, though continue to 
slowly cure. That said, the offset of highest winds and lowest 
humidity along with the mainly green fuels will keep fire danger 
capped at high. Fire danger will come to an end Saturday evening as 
humidity increases. Winds will slowly weaken through the evening and 
overnight hours, continuing another night of mild low temperatures 
in the 60s. These low temperatures will again come close to record 
warm lows.

Warm temperatures will continue through Sunday though not as warm as 
a cold front begins to push into the forecast area from the 
northwest. Medium range guidance continues to vary on how quickly 
the front pushes through the forecast area. Winds will remain breezy 
but much weaker than Saturday's winds. Humidity will be lower, 
though above critical thresholds, so some elevated fire danger 
remains possible. 

An upper level trough will dive across the west coast on Monday 
before beginning to eject into the Plains late Tuesday and 
Wednesday. There remains significant variance in the evolution of 
this wave but the ensembles show a clearer picture with the closed 
low transitioning to an open wave as it pushes into the Plains. This 
will also push the highest probabilities for rain to the middle of 
next week. The ensembles show a 30-70% chance for rainfall totals to 
exceed a tenth of an inch Wednesday through Thursday. In addition to 
the chances for rain, temperatures will trend to near seasonable 
with highs in the 60s and low sin the 40s and 50s.
